title: Diversity against sampling, per stage

issues.text: A correlation can't say which way it runs: rich stages may have more genera because there were more dinosaurs, or more finds because more beds of that age are exposed and dug.
issues.fix: Read rho as a warning about the raw curve, not as a cause.

issues.text: 29 stages is a small sample, and neighbouring stages share genera (range-through).
issues.fix: Report rho with its interval; a subsampled curve (shareholder quorum subsampling) is the real correction.

alternatives.question: Does the drop in genera found in the last stages of the Jurassic survive when each stage is cut to the same number of finds?
alternatives.why: Drills into the diversity curve: rarefaction against the finds table.

alternatives.question: Do theropods, sauropodomorphs and ornithischians rise and fall together across the stages?
alternatives.why: Drills into the groups, with the genus table already on the board.

alternatives.question: Did mammals, pterosaurs and marine reptiles lose as many genera at the K–Pg boundary as dinosaurs did?
alternatives.why: Expands to the other groups of the time: the big five extinctions.

question: Does the number of dinosaur genera found per stage follow the number of finds per stage?

hypotheses.statement: Stages with more fossil finds have more genera found in them.
hypotheses.null: Genera found per stage don't rise with finds per stage.

method.summary: Rank correlation of genera found and finds over the 29 stages.

steps.title: Genera and finds per stage from PBDB's diversity service
Spearman's rho between the two columns
A strong positive rho: read the diversity curve with the sampling panel beside it

caveats: Stages differ in length (from about 2 to 12 million years): longer stages hold more of both.
Finds are counted at genus level; one rich quarry can dominate a stage.
Range-through counts fill gaps between a genus' first and last find; the found counts don't.
